nodes.title: 🧩 1. Model Setup
widgets_values:
### Model References
Load the following models before running the workflow:

- **UNet (Main Model)**  
  [Qwen-Image-Edit-2509-Q6_K.gguf](https://huggingface.co/QuantStack/Qwen-Image-Edit-2509-GGUF/blob/main/Qwen-Image-Edit-2509-Q6_K.gguf)

- **CLIP Text Encoder**  
  [qwen_2.5_vl_7b_fp8_scaled.safetensors](https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/Qwen-Image_ComfyUI/blob/main/split_files/text_encoders/qwen_2.5_vl_7b_fp8_scaled.safetensors)

- **VAE**  
  [qwen_image_vae.safetensors](https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/Qwen-Image_ComfyUI/blob/main/split_files/vae/qwen_image_vae.safetensors)

- **LoRA**  
  [Qwen-Image-Lightning-4steps-V2.0-bf16.safetensors](https://huggingface.co/lightx2v/Qwen-Image-Lightning/blob/main/Qwen-Image-Lightning-4steps-V2.0-bf16.safetensors)

nodes.title: ⚙️ 2. Controls & Resolution
widgets_values:
- **Recommended Base Resolution:** `1328 × 1328`  
  Avoid changing this value to maintain optimal compatibility with the model’s architecture and latent scaling.

- **Sampler & Scheduler ([RES4LYF](https://github.com/ClownsharkBatwing/RES4LYF)):**  
  - **Sampler:** `res_2s`  
  - **Scheduler:** `beta57`  
  - **Steps:** 4 (default)  
    - Sometimes, **3 steps** gives results closer to the reference face, though it may occasionally produce incomplete generations.

- **Mask Color:**  
  Use **magenta (`221, 59, 207`)** as the mask color.  
  This color is rarely present in images and works reliably with the inpainting prompt logic.

nodes.title: 🖼️ 3. Reference Images
widgets_values:
### Face Reference
- Use **close-up images** with the subject looking **directly at the camera**.  
- Prefer **neutral facial expressions** — avoid smiles or exaggerated expressions.  
- The clearer and more frontal the face, the better the swap alignment.

### Body Reference
- Avoid images where the person is **too far from the camera**; distant faces are harder to detect.  
- Avoid images with **multiple people**, unless you manually mask the correct target.  
- Use well-lit, natural environments whenever possible.

### Matching Tips
For best results:
- Choose **face and body references** with **similar skin tones** — this helps the lighting and tone blending look natural.  
- Try to match **face shapes** (e.g., round, oval, angular) between both images.  
  This ensures a more realistic fusion and avoids distortions around the jawline and cheeks.

nodes.title: 🎭 4. Masks
widgets_values:
### Important Notes
- For **head swaps**, enable segmentation of both **face and hair** in the node **“Body Reference Face Segmentation.”**  
- For **face-only swaps**, enable only the **face segmentation.**

### Common Mask Issues
- If parts of the face are obscured (e.g., a hand over the mouth or eyes), segmentation may fail to cover small regions such as gaps between fingers.  
  - To fix this, increase the `fill_holes` parameter in the **Mask Fix** node.  
  - Alternatively, refine the mask manually.

### Planar Face Overlay (Optional Tool)
- A custom node created to assist with **alignment**, **skin tone correction**, and **face flipping.**  
- It serves as a backup method when the standard face-swap nodes do not produce satisfactory results.

You can switch to the **Planar Face Overlay outputs** by toggling these switches:
- `Body Face Mask`
- `Face Cropped`
- `Pose Map`

Each of these defaults to `true` (standard method).  
Set to `false` only if you want to use the **Planar Overlay outputs** instead.

nodes.title: 🔧 5. Core Processing
widgets_values:
### Pose Map Influence
The **pose map** can improve the match between the body and face orientation.  
However:
- It sometimes alters facial proportions (eye spacing, jawline, etc.), making the result less faithful to the face reference.
- If the resemblance decreases, **disconnect the “pose_map” input** from the **Qwen Text Encode Custom** node.

A reroute node is placed in front of the input for easy disconnection when needed.

> 💡 Tip: Use pose maps only when both the face and body reference are similar in orientation and lighting.

---

### Ollama Describer Integration
This workflow includes the **Ollama Describer** node, which extracts facial expression and pose details from the body reference image.  
These details are used to dynamically enrich the prompt for Qwen, enhancing realism and consistency.

You can replace this with any node capable of analyzing an image and generating textual descriptions (e.g., Qwen-VL, Gemini, Florence2, etc.).

---

### Inpainting Strategy
The inpainting method applies generation **only inside the masked region**, preserving all other image areas untouched.  
This ensures the rest of the image (environment, lighting, etc.) remains consistent with the original body reference.

Auxiliary nodes like:
- **Reference Latent**
- **Differential Diffusion**

…help maintain local detail consistency and improve blending quality.

---

### Troubleshooting Tips
If the result looks off:
1. Change the **seed** and re-generate.  
2. Try toggling the **pose map** on/off.  
3. As a last resort, use the **Planar Face Overlay** masks and outputs.

---

nodes.title: 🔁 6. Batch Automation (Optional)
widgets_values:
You can automate the workflow to process **multiple body reference images** in sequence.

### How to Set It Up
Use the following nodes with **bypass enabled**:
- `For Each Filename`  
- `Load Image From Path`  
- `For Each`

### Steps
1. In the **For Each Filename** node, set the folder path that contains your body reference images.  
2. Connect the **Image** output from `Load Image From Path` to the **Resize Body** node that receives the body reference input.  
3. Run the workflow multiple times — once per image.  
   - For example, if you have **20 images**, run it **20 times**.  
   - The workflow will automatically load one image per iteration and perform the full face-swap process.

This setup allows quick looping over entire folders without manual reloading, perfect for dataset generation or batch testing.

nodes.title: 🌐 Overview
widgets_values:

**Created by:** Alisson Anjos (aka **NRDX**)
**Profiles:**

* 🔗 [Civitai – NRDX](https://civitai.com/user/NRDX)
* 🔗 [Hugging Face – Alissonerdx](https://huggingface.co/Alissonerdx)

I spent about **two weeks refining this workflow**, testing different ideas and node combinations.
I also spent a lot of time trying to solve the **skin tone consistency issue** — which is still a challenge — but I couldn’t completely fix it yet.

Even so, this version goes beyond the usual simple face-swap setups.
While basic workflows can work to some extent, **this workflow** is built to be more **precise, stable, and automated**, giving you better control and cleaner results without constant manual adjustments.

---

If you want the pose map to be used, you can connect it to the pose map input. This makes it follow the pose of the face elements more closely, but it can make it less similar to the reference image of the face, as it will influence the distance between the eyes and between the nose and mouth, changing the physiognomy.

nodes.title: Second Option
widgets_values:
You are given an image.
Describe the scene in one concise, photorealistic sentence.

Rules:

* Describe only objective visual features related to facial expression, head orientation, gaze direction, and lighting.
* Include the person’s facial expression (neutral, smiling, serious, mouth open/closed, etc.).
* Include the head angle and pose (frontal, profile, slightly turned, tilted up/down, body posture if visible).
* Include the gaze direction (looking forward, left, right, up, down, off-camera).
* Mention the environment or lighting (e.g., indoor light, daylight, soft shadows, etc.).
* Do NOT describe:

  * skin tone, hair, beard, mustache, eyebrows, or any facial feature details
  * clothing, accessories, or objects
  * artistic or fantasy elements
  * gender, age, ethnicity, or resemblance to a known person
* Keep it neutral, factual, and strictly visual.

Examples (do not copy):

1. The person looks slightly to the left with a calm, neutral expression, head tilted down under soft indoor lighting.
2. The subject faces the camera in a frontal pose, smiling faintly while looking straight ahead in natural daylight.
3. The person is captured in profile, gaze directed upward with a focused expression against a blurred outdoor background.
4. The subject leans slightly forward, head tilted to the right, looking down with a serious expression under warm evening light.
5. The person faces slightly left with a relaxed half-smile, illuminated by bright daylight with soft shadows.
6. The subject looks off-camera to the right, lips closed and expression neutral, under cool studio lighting.
7. The person tilts their head slightly upward with a confident expression, eyes directed forward under natural morning light.
8. The subject faces frontally with a serious expression, looking slightly upward under diffused white indoor light.
9. The person sits upright, head slightly turned to the left, smiling gently while looking forward in a softly lit room.
10. The subject looks downward with a calm expression, head tilted gently to the side, illuminated by window light.

You are given an image.  
Describe the scene in one concise, photorealistic sentence.  

Rules:  
- Include the person’s facial expression (neutral, smiling, serious, mouth open/closed, etc.).  
- Include the head angle and pose (frontal, profile, slightly turned, tilted up/down, body posture if visible).  
- Include the gaze direction (looking forward, left, right, up, down, off-camera).  
- Mention general skin tone (fair, medium, dark, etc.).  
- Mention the environment, lighting, or background if visible.  
- Do not describe identity-level details like eye color, hair style, hair color, or eyebrows.  
- Keep it objective and visual.  

Examples (do not copy):

1. A woman with fair skin and brown hair looks slightly to the left with a calm, neutral expression, her head gently tilted down under soft indoor lighting.

2. A man with medium skin tone and black hair faces the camera in a frontal pose, smiling faintly while looking straight ahead in natural daylight.
